{{Short description|Study of optimal transportation and allocation of resources}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2021}}
In [[mathematics]] and economics, '''transportation theory''' or '''transport theory''' is a name given to the study of [[Optimization|optimal]] [[transport]]ation and [[Resource allocation|allocation of resources]]. The problem was formalized by the French [[mathematician]] [[Gaspard Monge]] in 1781.<ref name=Monge>G. Monge. ''Mémoire sur la théorie des déblais et des remblais. Histoire de l'Académie Royale des Sciences de Paris, avec les Mémoires de Mathématique et de Physique pour la même année'', pages 666–704, 1781.</ref>

In the 1920s A. N. Tolstoi was one of the first to study the transportation problem [[mathematical model|mathematically]]. In 1930, in the collection ''Transportation Planning Volume I'' for the National Commissariat of Transportation of the Soviet Union, he published a paper "Methods of Finding the Minimal Kilometrage in Cargo-transportation in space".<ref>[[Alexander Schrijver|Schrijver, Alexander]], [https://books.google.com/books?id=mqGeSQ6dJycC ''Combinatorial Optimization''], Berlin; New York : Springer, 2003. {{isbn|3540443894}}. Cf. [https://books.google.com/books?id=mqGeSQ6dJycC&dq=a.n.+tolstoi+transportation+networks&pg=PA362 p. 362]</ref><ref>Ivor Grattan-Guinness, Ivor,  [https://books.google.com/books?id=2hDvzITtfdAC ''Companion encyclopedia of the history and philosophy of the mathematical sciences''], Volume 1, JHU Press, 2003. Cf. [https://books.google.com/books?id=2hDvzITtfdAC&dq=%22a.n.+tolstoy%22+mathematics&pg=PA831 p.831]</ref>

Major advances were made in the field during [[World War II]] by the [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] mathematician and economist [[Leonid Kantorovich]].<ref name=Kantorovich>L. Kantorovich. ''On the translocation of masses.'' C.R. (Doklady) Acad. Sci. URSS (N.S.), 37:199–201, 1942.</ref> Consequently, the problem as it is stated is sometimes known as the '''Monge–Kantorovich transportation problem'''.<ref name="Villani2003">{{cite book|author=Cédric Villani|title=Topics in Optimal Transportation|year=2003|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-3312-4|page=66}}</ref> The [[linear programming]] formulation of the transportation problem is also known as the [[Frank Lauren Hitchcock|Hitchcock]]–[[Tjalling Koopmans|Koopmans]] transportation problem.<ref name="RaoRao2009">{{cite book|author1=Singiresu S. Rao|title=Engineering Optimization: Theory and Practice|year=2009|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-18352-6|page=221|edition=4th}}</ref>

==Motivation==

===Mines and factories===
[[File:Transport-plan.svg|thumb|Two one-dimensional distributions <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math>, plotted on the <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>. The two distributions can be pictured as two piles of dirt, one before moving, and one after moving. The heatmap in the center is a transport plan and denotes where each atom of dirt would be moved to.]]
Suppose that we have a collection of <math>m</math> mines mining iron ore, and a collection of <math>n</math> factories which use the iron ore that the mines produce. Suppose for the sake of argument that these mines and factories form two [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] [[subset]]s <math>M</math> and <math>F</math> of the [[Euclidean plane]] <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>. Suppose also that we have a ''cost function'' <math>c : \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2 \to [0, \infty)</math>, so that <math>c(x, y)</math> is the cost of transporting one shipment of iron from <math>x</math> to <math>y</math>. For simplicity, we ignore the time taken to do the transporting. We also assume that each mine can supply only one factory (no splitting of shipments) and that each factory requires precisely one shipment to be in operation (factories cannot work at half- or double-capacity). Having made the above assumptions, a ''transport plan'' is a [[bijection]] <math>T: M \to F</math>.
In other words, each mine <math>m \in M</math> supplies precisely one target factory <math>T(m) \in F</math> and each factory is supplied by precisely one mine. 
We wish to find the ''optimal transport plan'', the plan <math>T</math> whose ''total cost''
:<math>c(T) := \sum_{m \in M} c(m, T(m))</math>

is the least of all possible transport plans from <math>M</math> to <math>F</math>. This motivating special case of the transportation problem is an instance of the [[assignment problem]].
More specifically, it is equivalent to finding a minimum weight matching in a [[bipartite graph]].

This can be generalized to the continuous case, where there are infinitely many mines and factories distributed on the real line, or generally in any metric space. This case is usually pictured as "changing the shape of a pile of dirt", and thus called the [[Earth mover's distance|earth mover's problem]].

===Moving books: the importance of the cost function===
The following simple example illustrates the importance of the [[Cost curve|cost function]] in determining the optimal transport plan. Suppose that we have <math>n</math> books of equal width on a shelf (the [[real line]]), arranged in a single contiguous block. We wish to rearrange them into another contiguous block, but shifted one book-width to the right. Two obvious candidates for the optimal transport plan present themselves:
# move all <math>n</math> books one book-width to the right ("many small moves");
# move the left-most book <math>n</math> book-widths to the right and leave all other books fixed ("one big move").
If the cost function is proportional to [[Euclidean distance]] (<math>c(x, y) = \alpha \|x - y\|</math> for some <math>\alpha > 0</math>) then these two candidates are ''both'' optimal. If, on the other hand, we choose the [[Convex function|strictly convex]] cost function proportional to the square of Euclidean distance (<math>c(x, y) = \alpha \|x - y\|^2</math> for some <math>\alpha > 0</math>), then the "many small moves" option becomes the unique minimizer.

Note that the above cost functions consider only the horizontal distance traveled by the books, not the horizontal distance traveled by a device used to pick each book up and move the book into position. If the latter is considered instead, then, of the two transport plans, the second is always optimal for the Euclidean distance, while, provided there are at least 3 books, the first transport plan is optimal for the squared Euclidean distance.

=== Hitchcock problem ===
The following transportation problem formulation is credited to [[F. L. Hitchcock]]:<ref>Frank L. Hitchcock (1941) "The distribution of a product from several sources to numerous localities", [[MIT Journal of Mathematics and Physics]] 20:224–230 {{MR|id=0004469}}.
</ref>
:Suppose there are <math>m</math> sources <math>x_1, \ldots, x_m</math> for a commodity, with <math>a(x_i)</math> units of supply at <math>x_i</math> and <math>n</math> sinks <math>y_1, \ldots, y_n</math> for the commodity, with the demand <math>b(y_j)</math> at <math>y_j</math>. If <math>c(x_i,\ y_j)</math> is the unit cost of shipment from <math>x_i</math> to <math>y_j</math>, find a flow that satisfies demand from supplies and minimizes the flow cost. This challenge in logistics was taken up by [[D. R. Fulkerson]]<ref>D. R. Fulkerson (1956) [https://priorart.ip.com/IPCOM/000128834/ Hitchcock Transportation Problem], RAND corporation.</ref> and in the book ''Flows in Networks'' (1962) written with [[L. R. Ford Jr.]]<ref>[[L. R. Ford Jr.]] & [[D. R. Fulkerson]] (1962) § 3.1 in ''Flows in Networks'', page 95, [[Princeton University Press]]</ref>

[[Tjalling Koopmans]] is also credited with formulations of [[transport economics]] and allocation of resources.

==Abstract formulation of the problem==

===Monge and Kantorovich formulations===

The transportation problem as it is stated in modern or more technical literature looks somewhat different because of the development of [[Riemannian geometry]] and [[measure theory]]. The mines-factories example, simple as it is, is a useful reference point when thinking of the abstract case. In this setting, we allow the possibility that we may not wish to keep all mines and factories open for business, and allow mines to supply more than one factory, and factories to accept iron from more than one mine.

Let <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> be two [[separable space|separable]] [[metric space]]s such that any [[probability measure]] on <math>X</math> (or <math>Y</math>) is a [[Radon measure]] (i.e. they are [[Radon space]]s). Let <math>c : X \times Y \to [0, \infty)</math> be a Borel-[[measurable function]]. Given probability measures <math>\mu</math> on <math>X</math> and <math>\nu</math> on <math>Y</math>, Monge's formulation of the optimal transportation problem is to find a transport map <math>T : X \to Y</math> that realizes the [[infimum]]

:<math>\inf \left\{ \left. \int_X c(x, T(x)) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (x) \right| T_* (\mu) = \nu \right\},</math>

where <math>T_*(\mu)</math> denotes the [[pushforward measure|push forward]] of <math>\mu</math> by <math>T</math>. A map <math>T</math> that attains this infimum (''i.e.'' makes it a [[minimum]] instead of an infimum) is called an "optimal transport map".

Monge's formulation of the optimal transportation problem can be ill-posed, because sometimes there is no <math>T</math> satisfying <math>T_*(\mu) = \nu </math>: this happens, for example, when <math>\mu</math> is a [[Dirac measure]] but <math>\nu</math> is not.

We can improve on this by adopting Kantorovich's formulation of the optimal transportation problem, which is to find a probability measure <math>\gamma</math> on <math>X \times Y</math> that attains the infimum

:<math>\inf \left\{ \left. \int_{X \times Y} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) \right| \gamma \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu) \right\},</math>

where <math> \Gamma (\mu, \nu) </math> denotes the collection of all probability measures on <math>X \times Y</math> with [[Conditional probability|marginals]] <math>\mu</math> on <math>X</math> and <math>\nu</math> on <math>Y</math>.

=== Cost duality ===
[[File:C-transformation of a gaussian curve.svg|thumb|Example ''c''-duality transform, where ''<nowiki>c(x, y) = 2(cos(3x) + 1)|y − x|² + (4 − 2(cos(3x) + 1))|y − x|⁴</nowiki>'' and <math>\psi(x) = -e^{-x^2}</math>.]]Given a cost function <math>c(x, y)</math>, it produces a duality transformation <math>\psi \mapsto \psi^c</math> defined by<math display="block">\psi^c(y) := \inf_x (c(x, y) - \psi(x)) </math>This generalizes [[Legendre transformation]], which is the case where <math>c(x, y) = -xy</math> with a sign flip.
[[File:Infimal_convolution_of_a_cone_with_a_cubic_curve.svg|thumb|The ''c''-convexification of a curve in the case where <math>c(x,y) = |x-y|</math>.]]
<math>\leq 1</math>.

We say that a function <math>\psi</math> is '''''c''-convex''' if <math>\psi = \varphi^c</math> for some <math>\varphi</math>. Note that because <math>\varphi^{ccc} = \varphi^c  </math>, we can always assume that <math>\varphi</math> is ''c''-convex. The '''''c''-convexification''' of a function <math>\psi   </math> is <math>\psi^{cc}   </math>. Equivalently, it is the smallest ''c''-convex function <math>\psi'   </math> such that <math>\psi'\geq \psi   </math> pointwise.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Prop. 5.8}} Like in the case of convex transformation, <math>\psi</math> is ''c''-convex iff <math>\psi = \psi^{cc}</math>.

If <math>\psi = \varphi^c: X \to \R</math> is ''c''-convex, then the set of '''''c''-subdifferential''' of <math>\psi</math> at <math>x\in X</math> is the set of <math>y \in Y</math> such that <math>\psi(x) = c(x, y) - \varphi(y)</math>. Similarly for <math>Y</math>.

When <math>X = Y</math>, the graph <math>(y, \psi^c(y)) </math> can be constructed as follows: Take the graph of <math>\psi</math>, and flip it upside down. At each point <math>(x, -\psi(x))</math>, construct a graph of <math>y \mapsto c(x, y)</math> apexed at <math>(x, -\psi(x))</math>. That is, it is the graph of <math>y \mapsto c(x, y) - \psi(x)</math>. We obtain a whole set of such graphs. Their lower-edge [[Envelope (mathematics)|envelope]] is the graph of <math>\psi^c</math>.

In the same image, we can see what it means for a function <math>\varphi(y)   </math> to be ''c''-convex. It is ''c''-convex iff its entire graph can be "touched" by a "[[tipped tool]]" that is moving and shape-shifting. When the tipped tool is at <math>x</math>, it has a shape of <math>y \mapsto c(x, y)</math> and is raised to a height of <math>-\psi(x)</math>. The graph of the ''c''-convexification <math>\varphi^{cc}(y)   </math> is constructed by running the tipped tool so that it is lowered as much as possible, while still touching graph of <math>\varphi(y)   </math> on the upper side. The lower envelope swept out by the tipped tool is the graph of <math>\varphi^{cc}(y)   </math>.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Fig. 5.2}}

For example, if <math>X = Y = \R^n</math> is a metric space and <math>c(x, y) = \|x-y\|</math>, then <math>\varphi: X\to \R</math> is ''c''-convex iff it is 1-[[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz]]. This is used in the definition of 1-[[Wasserstein distance]]. If <math>c(x, y) = \|x-y\|^2</math>, then <math>\varphi</math> is ''c''-convex iff its graph could be touched from above by a tipped tool with the shape of a [[paraboloid]].

=== Existence and uniqueness ===


Under fairly permissive assumptions, optimal transport plan exists.<blockquote>If

* <math>(X, \mu_X), (Y, \mu_Y)</math> are [[Polish space|Polish probability spaces]],
* <math>c : X \times Y \to \R \cup\{\infty\}</math> is [[lower semicontinuous]], 
* and there exists some upper semicontinuous functions <math>a \in L^1(\mu_X), b \in L^1(\mu_Y)</math> of type <math>a: X \to \R\cup \{-\infty\},\; b: Y \to \R \cup \{-\infty\} </math> such that <math>c(x, y) \geq a(x) + b(y)</math>,

then an optimal transport ''plan'' exists. That is, exists <math>\gamma^* \in \Gamma(\mu_X, \mu_Y) </math> such that it reaches the infimum.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 4.1}}</blockquote>Note that the infimum could be infinite if all transport plans turn out to be infinite. For example, if <math>X = Y = \R, c(x, y) = |x-y|, \; \mu_X </math> is the [[Cauchy distribution]], and <math>\mu_Y = \delta_0 </math>.<blockquote>If

* <math>(X, \mu_X), (Y, \mu_Y)</math> are Polish probability spaces,
* <math>c : X \times Y \to \R</math> is lower semicontinuous,
* there exists some upper semicontinuous functions <math>a \in L^1(\mu_X), b \in L^1(\mu_Y)</math> of type <math>a: X \to \R,\; b: Y \to \R </math> such that <math>c(x, y) \geq a(x) + b(y)</math>,
* there exists a finite-cost transport plan,
* and for any ''c''-convex function <math>\psi: X \to \R \cup \{\infty\} </math>, for <math>\mu_X </math>-almost all <math>x\in X </math>, <math>\psi </math> has a unique ''c''-subdifferential at <math>x </math>

then an optimal transport ''map'' exists.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 5.30}}</blockquote>A restriction of an optimal transport plan is still optimal. That is, suppose <math>\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu) </math> is optimal, and <math>0 < \gamma' < \gamma </math>, and define the normalized transport plan <math>\bar\gamma' := \gamma' / \gamma'(X \times Y) </math>, then <math>\bar \gamma' </math> is an optimal transport plan between its own marginals.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 4.6}} If <math>\bar \gamma' </math> isn't optimal, then there exists an improvement of it, which then translates back to an improvement of the original <math>\gamma</math>.

=== Kantorovich duality ===

The '''Kantorovich duality''' states that:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=Optimal Transport: Old and New |date=2009 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-71049-3 |editor-last=Berger |editor-first=M. |series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |editor-last2=Serre |editor-first2=D. |editor-last3=Sinaj |editor-first3=Jakov G. |editor-last4=Sloane |editor-first4=N. J. A. |editor-last5=Vershik |editor-first5=A. M. |editor-last6=Villani |editor-first6=Cédric |editor-last7=Waldschmidt |editor-first7=M. |editor-last8=Eckmann |editor-first8=B. |editor-last9=Harpe |editor-first9=P.}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Thm. 5.10}}<blockquote>If <math>(X, \mu_X), (Y, \mu_Y)</math> are [[Polish space|Polish probability spaces]], <math>c : X \times Y \to \R \cup\{\infty\}</math> is [[lower semicontinuous]], and there exists some upper semicontinuous functions <math>a \in L^1(\mu_X), b \in L^1(\mu_Y)</math> of type <math>a: X \to \R,\; b: Y \to \R </math> such that <math>c(x, y) \geq a(x) + b(y)</math>, then<math display="block">\inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu) } \left( \int_{X \times Y} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) \right)
=
\sup_{\varphi \text{ is }c\text{-convex}} \left( \int_X \varphi (x) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (x) + \int_Y \varphi^c (y) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (y) \right)</math>If furthermore, <math>c</math> only takes real values, there exists a transport plan with finite cost, and there exists some functions <math>a' \in L^1(\mu_X), b' \in L^1(\mu_Y) </math> such that <math>c(x, y) \leq a'(x) + b'(y)</math>, then<math display="block">\min_{\gamma \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu) } \left( \int_{X \times Y} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) \right)
=
\max_{\varphi \text{ is }c\text{-convex}} \left( \int_X \varphi (x) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (x) + \int_Y \varphi^c (y) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (y) \right)</math></blockquote>Consider the second case, where we can actually arrive at an exactly optimal plan, instead of merely getting closer and closer. In this case, an optimal transport plan <math>\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu)</math>, constrains the form of an optimal pricing pair <math>(\varphi, \psi)</math>, and vice versa.

Given such an optimal pricing pair <math>(\varphi, \psi)</math>,<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Remark 5.13}}

* given an arbitrary transport plan <math>\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu)</math>, if all <math>(x, y) \in \operatorname{supp}(\gamma)</math> satisfies the exact equality <math>c(x, y) = \varphi(x) + \psi(y)</math>, then <math>\gamma</math> is an optimal plan;
* given an optimal transport plan <math>\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu)</math>, any <math>(x, y) \in \operatorname{supp}(\gamma)</math> must satisfy the exact equality <math>c(x, y) = \varphi(x) + \psi(y)</math>.
More succinctly, a transport plan is optimal iff it is supported on the set of ''c''-subdifferential pairs of <math>(\varphi, \psi)</math>.

=== Stability ===
The optimal transportation is ''stable'' in the following sense:<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 5.20}}<blockquote>Assume that <math>(X, \mu), (Y, \nu)</math> are [[Polish space|Polish probability spaces]], <math>c : X \times Y \to \R</math> is continuous, and <math>\inf c </math> is finite. Given a sequence of continuous functions <math>c : X \times Y \to \R</math> converging uniformly to <math>c</math> over <math>X \times Y</math>, a sequence <math>\mu_k \to \mu</math> weakly, a sequence <math>\nu_k \to \nu</math> weakly, and a sequence of optimal transport plans <math>\gamma_k \in \Gamma(\mu_k, \nu_k)</math>.

If the transport costs <math>\int c_k d\pi_k</math> satisfy <math>\int c_k d\pi_k < +\infty, \; \forall k</math> and <math>\liminf_k \int c_k d\pi_k < +\infty</math>, then <math>\gamma_k</math> converges weakly to some <math>\gamma</math>, and <math>\gamma</math> is an optimal transport plan from <math>\mu</math> to <math>\nu</math>.</blockquote>Similarly, the optimal transport map is also stable.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Cor. 5.23}}<blockquote>Assume that <math>(X, \mu), (Y, \nu)</math> are [[Polish space|Polish probability spaces]], <math>X</math> is locally compact, <math>c : X \times Y \to \R</math> is lower semicontinuous, and <math>\inf c </math> is finite. Given a sequence of lower semicontinuous functions <math>c : X \times Y \to \R</math> converging uniformly to <math>c</math> over <math>X \times Y</math>, a sequence <math>\nu_k \to \nu</math> weakly, </blockquote>

===Economic interpretation===

The optimal transport problem has an economic interpretation.<ref name="Galichon2016" /> [[Cédric Villani]] recounts the following interpretation from [[Luis Caffarelli]]:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Villani |first=Cédric |title=Topics in optimal transportation |date=2003 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8218-3312-X |location=Providence, RI |chapter=1.1.3. The shipper's problem. |oclc=51477002}}</ref><blockquote>Suppose you want to ship some coal from mines, distributed as <math>\mu</math>, to factories, distributed as <math>\nu</math>. The cost function of transport is <math>c</math>. Now a shipper comes and offers to do the transport for you. You would pay him <math>f(x)</math> per coal for loading the coal at <math>x</math>, and pay him <math>g(y)</math> per coal for unloading the coal at <math>y</math>. 

For you to accept the deal, the price schedule must satisfy <math>f(x) + g(y) \leq c(x, y)</math>. The Kantorovich duality states that the shipper can make a price schedule that makes you pay almost as much as you would ship yourself.</blockquote>In the interpretation, the duality transformation transforms a loading cost function <math>\varphi(x)</math> into the optimal (for the shipper) unloading cost function <math>\psi(y) = \varphi^c(y)</math>. If the unloading cost function <math>\psi(y)</math> were any higher at any point, then there would be some route <math>x \to y</math> on which <math>c(x, y) < \varphi(x) + \psi(y)</math>, meaning that there is some route on which you would rather ship yourself. But if the unloading cost function were any lower at any point, then the shipper could have earned more money by raising the price there. Therefore, the shipper should always choose <math>\psi = \varphi^c</math>. The same argument applied again then states that the shipper should always choose <math>\varphi = \psi^c</math>, and therefore we obtain the lower bound half of the duality formula:<math display="block">\inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu) } \left( \int_{X \times Y} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) \right)
\geq
\sup_{\varphi \text{ is }c\text{-convex}} \left( \int_X \varphi (x) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (x) + \int_Y \varphi^c (y) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (y) \right),</math>The Kantorovich duality states that it is in fact an equality, i.e. the shipper can make you pay as much as you would pay yourself, though the shipper might never exactly reach the bound (thus the use of infimum and supremum, instead of minimum and maximum).

Assume that the shipper in fact must pay the same cost function and us, and can exactly reach the maximum revenue using <math>(\varphi, \psi)</math> as their pricing chart. Then the shipper must use an optimal plan, at which point the shipper just breaks even with no profit. Conversely, any shipping plan that allows the shipper to exactly break even must be optimal.

==Solution of the problem==

===Optimal transportation on the real line===
{{multiple image

For <math>1 \leq p < \infty</math>, let <math>\mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})</math> denote the collection of [[probability measure]]s on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> that have finite <math>p</math>-th [[moment (mathematics)|moment]]. Let <math>\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})</math> and let <math>c(x, y) = h(x-y)</math>, where <math>h:\mathbb{R} \to [0,\infty)</math> is a [[convex function]].
# If <math>\mu</math> has no [[atom (measure theory)|atom]], i.e., if the [[cumulative distribution function]] <math>F_\mu : \mathbb{R}\to[0,1]</math> of <math>\mu</math> is a [[continuous function]], then <math>F_{\nu}^{-1} \circ F_{\mu} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}</math> is an optimal transport map. It is the unique optimal transport map if <math>h</math> is strictly convex.
# We have
::<math>\min_{\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) = \int_0^1 c \left( F_{\mu}^{-1} (s), F_{\nu}^{-1} (s) \right) \, \mathrm{d} s.</math>

The proof of this solution appears in Rachev & Rüschendorf (1998).<ref name=RL_MTP>Rachev, Svetlozar T., and Ludger Rüschendorf. ''Mass Transportation Problems: Volume I: Theory''. Vol. 1. Springer, 1998.</ref>

===Discrete version and linear programming formulation===

In the case where the margins <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> are discrete, let <math>\mu_x</math>
and <math>\nu_y</math> be the probability masses respectively assigned to <math>x\in \mathbf{X}</math> and <math>y\in \mathbf{Y}</math>, and let <math>\gamma_{xy}</math> be the probability of an <math>xy</math> assignment. The objective function in the primal Kantorovich problem is then

: <math> \sum_{x\in \mathbf{X},y\in \mathbf{Y}} \gamma_{xy}c_{xy}</math>

and the constraint <math>\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu ,\nu)</math> expresses as

: <math>
\sum_{y\in \mathbf{Y}}\gamma_{xy}=\mu_x,\forall x\in \mathbf{X}
</math>
and
: <math>
\sum_{x\in \mathbf{X}} \gamma_{xy}=\nu_y,\forall y\in \mathbf{Y}.
</math>

In order to input this in a [[linear programming]] problem, we need to [[Vectorization (mathematics)|vectorize]] the matrix <math>\gamma_{xy}</math> by either stacking [[Row- and column-major order|its columns or its rows]], we call <math>\operatorname{vec}</math> this operation. In the [[Row- and column-major order|column-major order]], the constraints above rewrite as

: <math> \left( 1_{1\times |\mathbf{Y}| }\otimes I_{|\mathbf{X}|}\right) \operatorname{vec}(\gamma)=\mu</math> and <math> \left( I_{|\mathbf{Y}\|}\otimes 1_{1\times |\mathbf{X}|}\right) \operatorname{vec}(\gamma)=\nu</math>

where <math>\otimes</math> is the [[Kronecker product]], <math>1_{n\times m}</math> is a matrix of size <math>n\times m</math> with all entries of ones, and <math>I_{n}</math> is the [[identity matrix]] of size <math>n</math>. As a result, setting <math>z=\operatorname{vec}(\gamma) </math>, the linear programming formulation of the problem is

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \text{Minimize } &&\operatorname{vec}(c)^\top z \\[4pt]
& \text{subject to:} && z \ge 0, \\[4pt]
& && \begin{pmatrix}
1_{1\times |\mathbf{Y}|}\otimes I_{|\mathbf{X}|} \\
I_{|\mathbf{Y}|}\otimes 1_{1\times |\mathbf{X}|}
\end{pmatrix} z=\binom{\mu}{\nu}
\end{align}
</math>

which can be readily inputted in a large-scale linear programming solver (see chapter 3.4 of Galichon (2016)<ref name="Galichon2016">[[Alfred Galichon|Galichon, Alfred]]. ''Optimal Transport Methods in Economics''. Princeton University Press, 2016.</ref>).

===Semi-discrete case===

In the semi-discrete case, <math>X=Y=\mathbb{R}^d</math> and <math>\mu</math> is a continuous distribution over <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>, while <math>\nu =\sum_{j=1}^J \nu_j\delta_{y_i}</math> is a [[Probability distribution|discrete distribution]] which assigns probability mass <math>\nu_j</math> to site <math>y_j \in \mathbb{R}^d</math>. In this case, we can see<ref>Santambrogio, Filippo. ''Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians''. Birkhäuser Basel, 2016. In particular chapter 6, section 4.2.</ref> that the primal and dual Kantorovich problems respectively boil down to:
:<math> \inf \left\{ \int_X \sum_{j=1}^J c(x,y_j) \, d\gamma_j(x) ,\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu,\nu)\right\} </math>
for the primal, where <math>\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu ,\nu)</math> means that <math>\int_X d\gamma_j(x)=\nu_j</math> and <math>\sum_j d\gamma_j(x) =d\mu(x)</math>, and:
:<math> \sup \left\{ \int_X\varphi(x)d\mu (x)+\sum_{j=1}^J\psi_j\nu_j:\psi_j+\varphi (x)\leq c(x,y_j) \right\}</math>
for the dual, which can be rewritten as:
:<math> \sup_{\psi \in \mathbb{R}^J}\left\{ \int_X\inf_j\left\{ c(x,y_j)-\psi_j\right\} d\mu (x)+\sum_{j=1}^J\psi_j\nu_j\right\} </math>
which is a finite-dimensional [[convex optimization]] problem that can be solved by standard techniques, such as [[gradient descent]].

In the case when <math>c(x,y)=|x-y|^2/2</math>, one can show that the set of <math>x\in \mathbf{X}</math> assigned to a particular site <math>j</math> is a convex polyhedron. The resulting configuration is called a [[power diagram]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Aurenhammer | first = Franz | author-link = Franz Aurenhammer
 | doi = 10.1137/0216006
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Computing]]
 | mr = 873251
 | pages = 78–96
 | title = Power diagrams: properties, algorithms and applications
 | volume = 16
 | year = 1987}}.
</ref>

===Quadratic normal case===

Assume the particular case <math>\mu =\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_X)</math>, <math>\nu =\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma _{Y})</math>, and <math>c(x,y) =|y-Ax|^2/2</math> where <math>A</math> is invertible. One then has

: <math> \varphi(x) =-x^\top \Sigma_X^{-1/2}\left( \Sigma_X^{1/2}A^\top \Sigma_Y A\Sigma_X^{1/2}\right) ^{1/2}\Sigma_{X}^{-1/2}x/2 </math>

: <math> \psi(y) =-y^\top A\Sigma_X^{1/2}\left( \Sigma_X^{1/2}A^\top \Sigma_Y A\Sigma_{X}^{1/2}\right)^{-1/2} \Sigma_X^{1/2}Ay/2 </math>

: <math> T(x) = (A^\top)^{-1}\Sigma_X^{-1/2} \left(\Sigma_X^{1/2}A^\top \Sigma_Y A\Sigma_X^{1/2} \right)^{1/2} \Sigma_X^{-1/2}x </math>

The proof of this solution appears in Galichon (2016).<ref name="Galichon2016" />

===Separable Hilbert spaces===
Let <math>X</math> be a [[separable space|separable]] [[Hilbert space]]. Let <math>\mathcal{P}_p(X)</math> denote the collection of probability measures on <math>X</math> that have finite <math>p</math>-th moment; let <math>\mathcal{P}_p^r(X)</math> denote those elements <math>\mu \in \mathcal{P}_p(X)</math> that are '''Gaussian regular''': if <math>g</math> is any [[strictly positive measure|strictly positive]] [[Gaussian measure]] on <math>X</math> and <math>g(N) = 0</math>, then <math>\mu(N) = 0</math> also.

Let <math>\mu \in \mathcal{P}_p^r (X)</math>, <math>\nu \in \mathcal{P}_p(X)</math>, <math>c (x, y) = | x - y |^p/p</math> for <math>p\in(1,\infty), p^{-1} + q^{-1} = 1</math>. Then the Kantorovich problem has a unique solution <math>\kappa</math>, and this solution is induced by an optimal transport map: i.e., there exists a Borel map <math>r\in L^p(X, \mu; X)</math> such that

:<math>\kappa = (\mathrm{id}_X \times r)_{*} (\mu) \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu).</math>

Moreover, if <math>\nu</math> has [[bounded set|bounded]] [[support (measure theory)|support]], then

:<math>r(x) = x -  | \nabla \varphi (x) |^{q - 2} \, \nabla \varphi (x)</math>

for <math>\mu</math>-almost all <math>x\in X</math> for some [[Lipschitz continuous|locally Lipschitz]], <math>c</math>-concave and maximal Kantorovich potential <math>\varphi</math>. (Here <math>\nabla \varphi</math> denotes the [[Gateaux derivative]] of <math>\varphi</math>.)

=== By minimizing flows ===
A gradient descent formulation for the solution of the Monge–Kantorovich problem was given by [[Sigurd Angenent]], Steven Haker, and [[Allen Tannenbaum]].<ref name="AHT">{{cite journal |last1=Angenent |first1=S. |last2=Haker |first2=S. |last3=Tannenbaum |first3=A. |year=2003 |title=Minimizing flows for the Monge–Kantorovich problem |journal=SIAM J. Math. Anal. |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=61–97 |citeseerx=10.1.1.424.1064 |doi=10.1137/S0036141002410927}}</ref>

== Entropic regularization ==
Consider a variant of the discrete problem above, where we have added an entropic regularization term to the objective function of the primal problem

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \text{Minimize } \sum_{x\in \mathbf{X}, y\in \mathbf{Y}}\gamma_{xy}c_{xy}+\varepsilon \gamma_{xy} \ln \gamma_{xy} \\[4pt]
& \text{subject to: } \\[4pt]
& \gamma\ge0 \\[4pt]
& \sum_{y\in \mathbf{Y}}\gamma_{xy} = \mu_x, \forall x\in \mathbf{X} \\[4pt]
& \sum_{x\in \mathbf{X}}\gamma_{xy} = \nu_y, \forall y\in \mathbf{Y}
\end{align}
</math>

One can show that the dual regularized problem is

:<math>
\max_{\varphi ,\psi} \sum_{x\in \mathbf{X}} \varphi_x \mu_x + \sum_{y\in \mathbf{Y}} \psi_y v_y - \varepsilon \sum_{x\in \mathbf{X},y\in \mathbf{Y}} \exp \left( \frac{\varphi_x + \psi_y - c_{xy}}{\varepsilon }\right)
</math>

where, compared with the unregularized version, the "hard" constraint in the former dual (<math>\varphi_x + \psi_y - c_{xy}\geq 0</math>) has been replaced by a "soft" penalization of that constraint (the sum of the <math>\varepsilon \exp \left( (\varphi _x + \psi_y - c_{xy})/\varepsilon \right)</math> terms). The optimality conditions in the dual problem can be expressed as

:{{EquationRef|5.1|Eq. 5.1:}} <math>
\mu_x = \sum_{y\in \mathbf{Y}} \exp \left( \frac{\varphi_x + \psi_y - c_{xy}}{\varepsilon} \right) ~\forall x\in \mathbf{X}
</math>

:{{EquationRef|5.2|Eq. 5.2:}} <math>
\nu_y = \sum_{x\in \mathbf{X}} \exp \left( \frac{\varphi_x + \psi_y - c_{xy}}{\varepsilon }\right) ~\forall y\in \mathbf{Y}  
</math>

Denoting <math>A</math> as the <math>|\mathbf{X}| \times |\mathbf{Y}|</math> matrix of term <math>A_{xy}=\exp \left(-c_{xy} / \varepsilon \right)</math>, solving the dual is therefore equivalent to looking for two diagonal positive matrices <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> of respective sizes <math>|\mathbf{X}|</math> and <math>|\mathbf{Y}|</math>, such that <math>D_1AD_2 1_{|\mathbf{Y}|}=\mu</math> and <math>(D_1AD_2)^\top 1_{|\mathbf{X}|}=\nu </math>. The existence of such matrices generalizes [[Sinkhorn's theorem]] and the matrices can be computed using the [[Sinkhorn's theorem#Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm|Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm]],<ref>[[Gabriel Peyré|Peyré, Gabriel]] and Marco Cuturi (2019), "Computational Optimal Transport: With Applications to Data Science", Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning: Vol. 11: No. 5-6, pp 355–607. DOI: [http://dx.doi.org/10.1561/2200000073 ''10.1561/2200000073''].</ref> which simply consists of iteratively looking for <math>\varphi_x</math> to solve {{EquationNote|5.1|Equation 5.1}}, and <math>\psi_y</math> to solve {{EquationNote|5.2|Equation 5.2}}. Sinkhorn–Knopp's algorithm is therefore a [[coordinate descent]] algorithm on the dual regularized problem.

== Applications ==
The Monge–Kantorovich optimal transport has found applications in wide range in different fields. Among them are:
* [[Image registration]] and warping<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Haker|first1=Steven|last2=Zhu|first2=Lei|last3=Tannenbaum|first3=Allen|last4=Angenent|first4=Sigurd|date=1 December 2004|title=Optimal Mass Transport for Registration and Warping|journal=International Journal of Computer Vision|language=en|volume=60|issue=3|pages=225–240|doi=10.1023/B:VISI.0000036836.66311.97|issn=0920-5691|citeseerx=10.1.1.59.4082|s2cid=13261370}}</ref>
* Reflector design<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Glimm|first1=T.|last2=Oliker|first2=V.|date=1 September 2003|title=Optical Design of Single Reflector Systems and the Monge–Kantorovich Mass Transfer Problem|journal=Journal of Mathematical Sciences|language=en|volume=117|issue=3|pages=4096–4108|doi=10.1023/A:1024856201493|s2cid=8301248|issn=1072-3374}}</ref>
* Retrieving information from [[shadowgraph]]y and proton radiography<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kasim|first1=Muhammad Firmansyah|last2=Ceurvorst|first2=Luke|last3=Ratan|first3=Naren|last4=Sadler|first4=James|last5=Chen|first5=Nicholas|last6=Sävert|first6=Alexander|last7=Trines|first7=Raoul|last8=Bingham|first8=Robert|last9=Burrows|first9=Philip N.|author9-link=Philip N. Burrows|date=16 February 2017|title=Quantitative shadowgraphy and proton radiography for large intensity modulations|journal=Physical Review E|volume=95|issue=2|article-number=023306|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.95.023306|pmid=28297858|arxiv=1607.04179|bibcode=2017PhRvE..95b3306K|s2cid=13326345}}</ref>
* [[Seismic tomography]] and [[reflection seismology]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Metivier |first1=Ludovic |title=Measuring the misfit between seismograms using an optimal transport distance: application to full waveform inversion |journal=Geophysical Journal International |date=24 February 2016 |volume=205 |issue=1 |pages=345–377 |doi=10.1093/gji/ggw014 |bibcode=2016GeoJI.205..345M |url=https://academic.oup.com/gji/article-abstract/205/1/345/2594839|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* The broad class of [[Economics|economic]] modelling that involves gross substitutes property (among others, models of [[Stable matching theory|matching]] and [[discrete choice]]).
